title: Net Zero by 2050? This Decade's Fuel Choices Will Decide - The Maritime Executive
description:
Green-hydrogen based synthetic fuels are stalled by a coordination problem across industries.
First, hydrogen fuel production is a massive undertaking: renewable energy, electrolysis, synthesis plants, storage, pipelines, and ports.
In the absence of synthetic fuels, shipping is trying to juggle oil, diesel, liquefied natural gas, and biofuels.
Synthetic fuel contracts overturn every precedent: expensive, long-term, limited.
Both shipping and aviation giants have tried to make their own hydrogen and synthetic fuel supplies.
text:
Green-hydrogen based synthetic fuels are stalled by a coordination problem across industries. Pooling demand and investment across sectors could unlock the production scale needed for shipping and other hard-to-abate industries, while strengthening energy security in the transition to net zero.

The debate over whether net zero is possible by 2050 may continue for years, while global emissions and temperatures continue to rise. But the question of green hydrogen’s role in achieving it has swung from hype to skepticism to a pragmatic center: shipping and several other hard-to-abate sectors need green hydrogen to reach net zero. Yet, the hydrogen itself remains elusive. Demand waits for supply. Supply waits for demand. It’s an ouroboros.

Technology ahead of fuel

Taking shipping as an example, the industry has innovated and invested in dual-fuel ships capable of running on both conventional fuels and synthetic ammonia or methanol – and these ships are already setting sail. Their engines are designed to use fuel as efficiently as possible: today to reduce emissions from fossil fuels, and in the future, to make the most efficient use of the more expensive synthetic ammonia and methanol.

The problem is that while ship technology ran ahead, the fuel front was stalling.

First, hydrogen fuel production is a massive undertaking: renewable energy, electrolysis, synthesis plants, storage, pipelines, and ports.

Second, the bill. To reach net zero by 2050, shipping alone will need 100 to 150 million tons of green hydrogen annually as feedstock, even at maximum efficiency across the sector. The hard-to-abate sectors together will need 500 to 600 million, an investment of $9 trillion.

So, just for the feedstock, shipping would need to fund $2 to 3 trillion upfront. Which sector can afford today to commit three trillion dollars for a fuel that will be ready in 5-10 years and require upfront purchase contracts of 10 to 15 years?

And yet, that’s the timeline: 25 years to 2050.

The snake eating its tail

Meanwhile, the collapse of hydrogen projects around the world proves that the challenge is more than isolated anomalies; it is systemic.

Underpinning shipping’s deadlocked fuel transition is a set of five tightly linked factors – fuel fragmentation, geography, finance, regulation, and port constraints, that reinforce each other.

First, fuels. In the absence of synthetic fuels, shipping is trying to juggle oil, diesel, liquefied natural gas, and biofuels. This hedging is rational, but it dilutes investment and prevents any single fuel from scaling. It would be comparable to an electric vehicle charging infrastructure with 12 different types of current, which thankfully isn’t the case, or there would probably be no electric vehicles.

Second: geography. Following the oil and gas model, hydrogen production is concentrated in a few nation-scale projects – some as large as half of Switzerland. For shipping, 80% of the global fleet operates on flexible routes. An early market that forces trade to reroute from 6,000 ports to a mere handful of fuel supply hubs will limit adoption. Aviation would face a similar challenge.

Third: finance. Shipping’s low-cost, low-margin business model is predicated on the universal availability of the cheapest fuel in the global mix. Synthetic fuel contracts overturn every precedent: expensive, long-term, limited.

Fourth: regulation. Shipping’s global regulation should be a strength. Global carbon pricing could level the playing field for the entire industry. However, that strength depends on a two-thirds vote from member states. With the onus on national governments and local producers to assemble subsidies, permits, materials, and financing, many are reticent to approve the carbon pricing that would force demand. Aviation faces a similar challenge.

Fifth: ports. Ports are already stretched for power, land, and trained operators. Most cannot justify investment in new bunkering systems without predictable supply and demand.

The ouroboros tightens, and every hard-to-abate sector faces some version of this deadlock loop.

Breaking the loop

There is one way to get the snake to release its tail: give it more to eat – with coordinated demand across sectors.

Both shipping and aviation giants have tried to make their own hydrogen and synthetic fuel supplies. Each industry has tried to pool demand within the industry. It hasn’t worked, because no single company or sector can carry the cost and scale of green hydrogen alone. The balance sheet requires multiple industries. Shared offtake produces contracts large enough to start building, and allows sequential planning. Shared risk makes early projects insurable, and shared infrastructure avoids duplication.

Competition across sectors is stalling production, but collaboration can enable it.

Chance or illusion?

The willingness to embrace cross-sector collaboration depends on whether fossil fuels are still regarded as the safer economic bet.

However, even the oil majors are beginning to question that assumption. Wood Mackenzie estimates that oil and gas production could fall nearly 40% by 2040 without hundreds of billions of dollars in new upstream investment. Oil companies therefore face the same dilemma as hydrogen producers: demand uncertainty is freezing investment on both sides of the energy transition.

In the Asia-Pacific region, that same uncertainty, combined with volatile fossil import supply, is accelerating the shift toward carbon-neutral energy security.

China made that decision before many others had even asked the question. It cornered the global market in critical mineral processing for clean technologies, overbuilt renewables that can now be converted into hydrogen and synthetic fuels, and scaled its shipbuilding industry within four decades. As with electric vehicles, China can absorb early fuel price differentials through subsidies and leverage its domestic market to drive costs down.

China’s integrated energy, industrial, and shipping policy is material to developing the cross-sector sequencing required to make the transition work. Despite its size, it is also bringing smaller, modular e-fuel facilities online faster and cheaper, with one unit producing over 300,000 tons of green ammonia per year, already on export to Asia Pacific and Europe.

In Japan, Korea, and Singapore, the focus is on imports. Utilities are committing to ammonia offtake under national energy strategies, allowing safety standards, terminals, and bunkering systems to develop ahead of shipping demand.

Meanwhile, the Chinese modular approach is already being exported to Brazil. Vast land availability and very low solar power costs give Brazil a strong advantage in exporting synthetic fuels, and the country is already developing the ports of Açu and Pecém as green hydrogen and e-fuel hubs for power generation, industry, and shipping.

Across these cases, the pattern is consistent: land-based sectors lead; investment, risk, infrastructure, and offtake are shared and publicly supported; shipping follows once the regulatory framework is in place.

The decade of decision

At a time when the global debate between reinvesting in fossil systems and accelerating a fossil-free future is hardening once again, which path is industry betting on?

Is net zero possible by 2050? That depends on the decisions taken in this decade. The trade-offs will be felt by the next generation, one way or the other.

The task for industry and institutions is to move beyond siloed efforts and coordinate demand, infrastructure and investment across sectors to build a secure, net-zero energy future.

description:

The project links digitalisation with fuel efficiency and emissions control for ship managers.
It forms part of the Global Maritime Technology Cooperation Centres Network Phase II programme, funded by the European Union and implemented by the International Maritime Organization.
For ship managers, the focus is on improving day-to-day decisions that affect fuel use, maintenance, and overall vessel efficiency.
Digital tools, beyond reporting, are increasingly part of how vessels are run, with direct implications for fuel cost, emissions performance, and asset management.
text:
A vessel trial in Mexico is putting AI-driven decision tools into daily ship operations. The project links digitalisation with fuel efficiency and emissions control for ship managers. This is a shift towards data-led performance at sea.

Shipowners are exploring ways to improve fuel efficiency while meeting emissions targets, and a new pilot in Mexico is testing how artificial intelligence can support that task in real operations.

Launched at Pichilingue Port, the project introduces an onboard system designed to support decision-making through real-time data and performance analysis. It forms part of the Global Maritime Technology Cooperation Centres Network Phase II programme, funded by the European Union and implemented by the International Maritime Organization.

The system integrates real-time fuel consumption monitoring, performance analytics, and operational planning support. For ship managers, the focus is on improving day-to-day decisions that affect fuel use, maintenance, and overall vessel efficiency.

The pilot was presented during a national workshop organised by the Maritime Technology Cooperation Centre for Latin America under the theme “Advancing Maritime Decarbonisation in Mexico: Energy Efficiency Technology and Innovation for a Sustainable Transition”. The event brought together maritime professionals to explore practical approaches aligned with the 2023 IMO greenhouse gas strategy.

The GMN Phase II programme is designed to test technologies in operational settings, generating data that can guide wider adoption across fleets. Beyond this pilot, demonstrations include port efficiency, wind-assisted propulsion, and retrofit solutions.

Digital tools, beyond reporting, are increasingly part of how vessels are run, with direct implications for fuel cost, emissions performance, and asset management.

North African countries are being urged to act swiftly to capture a strategic share of the emerging green shipping economy, as the International Maritime Organization prepares to take a critical decision on its Net Zero Framework.

text:
IMO Net Zero Framework could unlock US$11–12 billion annually to accelerate green shipping fuels.

Egypt and Morocco positioned at key trade routes with low cost renewables and port infrastructure.

Nearly 80% of regional green fuel projects remain stalled at concept stage due to financing gaps.

North African countries are being urged to act swiftly to capture a strategic share of the emerging green shipping economy, as the International Maritime Organization prepares to take a critical decision on its Net Zero Framework.

A new policy brief published by the Green Hydrogen Organisation highlights the region’s strong potential to become a global hub for green fuel bunkering, at a time when the maritime sector faces mounting pressure to decarbonise. The urgency has intensified following recent spikes in heavy fuel oil prices driven by instability in the Middle East, once again exposing the vulnerability of global shipping to fossil fuel shocks.

The proposed Net Zero Framework, if adopted, would establish a legally binding pathway to net zero emissions in shipping by 2050. It is expected to generate US$11–12 billion per year through a dedicated fund designed to incentivise the uptake of green fuels such as ammonia, methanol and e LNG.

North Africa stands out as a natural contender in this transition. Egypt and Morocco are located along two of the world’s most strategic maritime corridors, the Suez Canal and the Strait of Gibraltar, which together handle more than 12% of global trade.

The region also benefits from some of the lowest renewable energy costs globally, with solar power in Egypt priced at around US$0.02 per kWh. Both countries already have established fertiliser industries and extensive experience in ammonia handling at ports, creating a strong foundation for scaling green ammonia production.

Such expansion could deliver multiple benefits, including decarbonising domestic fertiliser production, supplying Europe’s growing demand for clean ammonia and positioning North African ports as refuelling hubs for vessels travelling between Asia and Europe.

Analysis of the International Energy Agency database identified 74 green fuel projects across North Africa, with 47 located at or near ports. However, nearly 80% of these projects remain at an early concept stage, with limited progress due to financing constraints.

Industry stakeholders point to the Net Zero Framework as a critical enabler that could unlock investment by providing both a clear demand signal and long term regulatory certainty. New modelling from the UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group and RMI shows that only a comprehensive mechanism combining carbon pricing, a capped surplus unit market and targeted incentives can create a viable investment environment for zero and near zero fuels.

Early progress is already visible in the region. Egypt’s East Port Said recently hosted the first green methanol bunkering operation in Africa and the Middle East, supplying a vessel operated by Maersk. The Suez Canal Authority has also introduced incentives to encourage green infrastructure development.

Meanwhile, Morocco has launched its Green Hydrogen Offer to support the development of a full value chain, with estimates indicating that cost effective green fuel bunkering could be achieved at the Tanger Med Port.

Despite these advances, stakeholders agree that the absence of a global demand signal remains the key barrier. Without predictable revenue streams and clear regulatory direction, large scale investments are unlikely to materialise.

As the IMO prepares to deliberate, governments across the Middle East and North Africa, particularly Egypt and Morocco, are being encouraged to back the Net Zero Framework as a decisive step towards unlocking the region’s green shipping potential.

title: World's First Ocean-Going Ammonia-Powered Ships Will Drastically Cut Emissions
description:
Antwerpen and Arlon are officially the world’s first ocean-going ammonia-powered vessels, and the shipping industry’s first gas carriers of their kind.
Now, its proprietary technology was key in designing and building the three cargo tanks of these new ammonia-powered ships.
According to Exmar, this ammonia dual-fuel technology was proven to cut CO2 emissions during navigation by up to 90 percent.
In terms of safety, the new ships feature an ammonia gas detector for real-time monitoring and an ammonia purge recovery unit, as part of a complex detection and mitigation system.
The first operational ammonia-powered vessels were mainly tugboats (small-scale vessels in general), and many of the bigger ones were conventional vessels retrofitted with ammonia dual-fuel solutions.
text:
Antwerpen and Arlon are officially the world’s first ocean-going ammonia-powered vessels, and the shipping industry’s first gas carriers of their kind. The two ships (part of a four-ship order) celebrated their naming ceremony HD Hyundai’s Ulsan shipyard and will be ready to enter service with their Belgian operator later this year.

The naming celebration of Antwerpen and Arlon (named after Belgian cities) is the culmination of an almost four-year development program initiated by Exmar and HD Hyundai. As an expert in ammonia and LPG transportation, Exmar was ready to take the next step and introduce dual-fuel gas carriers capable of cutting CO2 emission levels by up to 90%.

HD Hyundai was the perfect partner for this bold initiative. Exactly a decade ago, it delivered the world’s first methanol-powered petrochemical product carrier, and two years ago it launched the world’s first methanol-powered container ship, two industry premieres that confirmed the South Korean giant’s leading position in eco-friendly shipbuilding. Now, its proprietary technology was key in designing and building the three cargo tanks of these new ammonia-powered ships.

Antwerpen and Arlon are each 190-meter (623 feet) long, 30.4-meter (98 feet) wide, and 18.8-meter (62 feet) high. They’re fitted with 45,000-cubic meter cargo tanks and two 500-cubic meter deck tanks for transporting liquefied gas cargo such as ammonia and LPG, and they’re powered by dual-fuel engines.

According to Exmar, this ammonia dual-fuel technology was proven to cut CO2 emissions during navigation by up to 90 percent. On top of that, the new ships feature a selective catalytic reduction (SCR) system, specifically for reducing nitrogen oxide emissions, which further boosts their environmental performance.

In terms of safety, the new ships feature an ammonia gas detector for real-time monitoring and an ammonia purge recovery unit, as part of a complex detection and mitigation system.

Bringing to life a game-changing vessel like these two also implies a lot of work in terms of regulatory efforts. It wasn’t just about designing and building the ships and their cargo tanks, but also working with authorities in the field - Lloyd’s Register and the Administration – to set specific guidelines for using ammonia as fuel on gas carriers.

This is why the launch of Antwerpen and Arlon is an important milestone and step forward for green shipping globally. According to the Ammonia Energy Association, 140 ammonia-fueled vessels have been operational or ordered as of March, this year, with the addition of more than 300 ammonia-ready vessels.

The first operational ammonia-powered vessels were mainly tugboats (small-scale vessels in general), and many of the bigger ones were conventional vessels retrofitted with ammonia dual-fuel solutions.

By comparison, Antwerpen and Arlon were purpose-built for ammonia-powered navigation as gas carriers, which makes them not only unique in the industry, but a major step in terms of eco-friendly shipbuilding.

text:
Vale and Shandong Shipping Partner to Build First Ethanol-Fueled Bulk Carriers

The Brazilian mining company Vale has formed an agreement with China's Shandong Shipping Corporation to construct the first large ocean-going vessels designed to use ethanol as a primary fuel, according to The Maritime Executive. The deal involves 25-year contracts for two new ships, with an option for more.

These vessels represent an adaptation of the existing Guaibamax design and are part of a multi-fuel strategy. The ships will be 340 meters long with a 325,000-tonne capacity and will be capable of using methanol and heavy fuel oil in addition to ethanol. Their design also permits future conversion to use liquefied natural gas or ammonia.

The move follows earlier industry exploration of ethanol as a marine fuel. Other shipping companies and engine manufacturers have also been testing ethanol, noting it is easier to handle than some toxic and corrosive alternatives. Vale highlights that, considering the full fuel cycle, ethanol can reduce carbon emissions by approximately 90 percent compared to heavy fuel oil when using second-generation ethanol.

The new ethanol-powered ships will be similar to ten other dual-fuel vessels that Shandong is scheduled to deliver to Vale starting in 2027. This second generation of Guaibamax vessels will incorporate several energy efficiency improvements, including five rotor sails for wind-assisted propulsion, more efficient engines, and various hydrodynamic and electrical upgrades. Vale states this suite of technologies should reduce greenhouse gas emissions by about 15 percent compared to the current Guaibamax generation.

Vale's broader adoption of ethanol extends beyond shipping to include trials on trucks and locomotives within its logistics operations. The company's existing chartered fleet, which includes various generations of large bulk carriers, is already noted for its efficiency.

description:
Once again, it exposes just how vulnerable the world remains to fossil fuel price shocks.
North Africa could be at the heart of that new green shipping fuel transition.
Scaling up green ammonia production could simultaneously decarbonise their domestic fertiliser industries, supply Europe's growing clean ammonia demand, and turn North African ports into green bunkering hubs for vessels moving between Asia and Europe.
East Port Said hosted the first green methanol bunkering operation in Africa and the Middle East, supplying a Maersk container ship.
Morocco's Green Hydrogen Offer provides a framework for the value chain, and the estimates that green hydrogen-based fuels could be bunkered at Tanger Med for a cost-effective configuration.
text:
We have just published a new policy brief on North Africa's potential to become a major green fuel bunkering hub and supplier as the maritime sector seeks ways to transition to clean fuels. The timing could not be more urgent. The price of heavy fuel oil which most ships still rely on, has surged dramatically in recent weeks due to the crisis in the Middle East. Once again, it exposes just how vulnerable the world remains to fossil fuel price shocks. The good news is that the International Maritime Organisation reconvenes this month to consider how to change that. Member States will decide how to move forward on the Net-Zero Framework, a legally binding measure targeting net-zero emissions from shipping by 2050 that was delayed by a year last October. If adopted, it would generate 11-12 billion USD annually through a net-zero fund to incentivise the switch to green fuels like ammonia, methanol or e-LNG and begin to break the sector’s dependence on fossil fuels once and for all.

North Africa could be at the heart of that new green shipping fuel transition. Egypt and Morocco sit at two of the world's most critical maritime chokepoints, the Suez Canal and the Strait of Gibraltar, through which more than 12% of global trade flows. Their renewable energy costs are among the lowest in the world, with solar electricity in Egypt priced as low as 2 cents per kWh. Both countries are already Africa's largest fertiliser producers and deeply familiar with ammonia handling at ports. Scaling up green ammonia production could simultaneously decarbonise their domestic fertiliser industries, supply Europe's growing clean ammonia demand, and turn North African ports into green bunkering hubs for vessels moving between Asia and Europe.

Our analysis of the IEA database identified 74 projects across the region, with 47 of them at or near ports. But almost 80% remain at the concept stage and financing is the critical bottleneck. The NZF would help break that deadlock by sending a strong demand signal and providing the regulatory certainty the industry needs to move. New modelling published yesterday by UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group and RMI reinforces the point: only the NZF combining a carbon price, a capped surplus unit market and a reward mechanism for zero and near-zero fuels creates the conditions for an investable transition.

The foundations are already there. East Port Said hosted the first green methanol bunkering operation in Africa and the Middle East, supplying a Maersk container ship. The Suez Canal Authority is incentivising green infrastructure. Morocco's Green Hydrogen Offer provides a framework for the value chain, and the estimates that green hydrogen-based fuels could be bunkered at Tanger Med for a cost-effective configuration. What is missing is the demand signal and revenue certainty that only a global IMO NZF can provide.

The right choice for governments in MENA like Egypt and Morocco is clear: support the IMO Net Zero Framework.

text:
Mirage News

Mirage News

Research Explores Renewables, Infrastructure for Net-Zero Ships

Energy-maritime infrastructure will be needed to enable the transport and use of renewable fuels required by the global energy transition.

A collaboration between International Maritime Organization (IMO)'s Future Fuels and Technology project and GreenVoyage2050 programme; the World Maritime University (WMU); and the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) aims to assess the current status quo and support informed decision-making on the development of infrastructure required to enable the large-scale uptake of renewable fuels.

The first output of this energy and maritime sector collaboration will be a global study, including country-level case studies, providing insights into both global trends and national contexts.

The study, which was initiated during a virtual meeting (1 April), will provide:

Overview of global renewable fuel production, supply and demand, including future projections

Assessment of energy and maritime infrastructure needs, including ports and fuel supply chains

Identification of key challenges and opportunities for scaling up renewable fuel deployment

Recommendations on priority actions and long-term strategies to support the development of maritime infrastructure

Meeting the ambitions in IMO's GHG Strategy to reach net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping by or around 2050 will require scaling up global markets for renewable fuels (including sustainable biofuels and e-fuels) and building up their supply chains. This means deployment of renewable energy power infrastructure, renewable fuel production facilities, fuel transport and bunkering infrastructure, other port infrastructure such as shore power, as well as vessels capable of using and transporting these fuels.

The global analysis report is expected to be finalized by third quarter 2026, to include identified priority actions and practical pathways for scaling up renewable fuel supply chains and enabling infrastructure.

In parallel, selected national case studies will be undertaken to explore how these findings apply in specific country contexts.

Results from these case studies are expected to be released by the fourth quarter of 2026.

IMO's project teams will continue working closely with WMU and IRENA to guide the study and support the delivery of practical and policy-relevant findings.

The study reports will be published by IMO on the respective project and partner websites and presented to IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC).

text:
Written by Marine Log Staff

Brazilian mining giant Vale and Chinese shipping company Shandong Shipping Corporation have concluded an agreement for new ethanol-powered Guaibamax vessels, which are scheduled for delivery starting in 2029.

The agreement marks a milestone for global iron ore transport: this is the first time in the maritime industry that ethanol will be used as the primary fuel on an ocean-going vessel. With the potential to reduce carbon emissions by around 90% compared to the use of heavy fuel oil, commonly used in shipping, the initiative reinforces Vale’s goal to reducing its carbon emissions across the value chain and promoting decarbonization in the maritime sector, in line with ongoing discussions at the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

The agreement between Vale and Shandong includes 25-year contracts for the construction of two vessels, with an option for additional ships. The adoption of these second-generation Guaibamax vessels, which are 340 meters long and have a capacity of 325,000 tonnes, is part of the Brazilian mining company’s multi-fuel strategy. In addition to ethanol, these vessels will be capable of using methanol and heavy fuel oil, and their design also allows for conversion to use liquefied natural gas (LNG) or ammonia.

“Vale’s pioneering efforts towards decarbonization in maritime transport are guided by a strategy that combines flexibility and efficiency. ‘The use of ethanol as fuel in the ships that transport our ore, combined with the adoption of rotor sails to harness wind energy, places Vale in a unique position for the energy transition in global shipping over the coming decades, whilst driving similar initiatives in the sector’, says Rodrigo Bermelho, Vale’s Director of Shipping.

Considering the full fuel cycle from well to wake, ethanol can reduce carbon emissions by around 90% (in the case of second-generation ethanol) compared with heavy fuel oil. In addition to maritime transport, Vale’s adoption of ethanol in its logistics operations includes trials on trucks at its operations and on locomotives on the Vitória a Minas Railway.

Reducing emissions

The new ethanol-powered ships will be similar to 10 other dual-fuel vessels (methanol and heavy fuel oil) that Shandong will deliver to Vale from 2027 onwards. The second generation of the Guaibamax will be equipped with five rotor sails—which harnesses wind energy to reduce fuel consumption—more efficient engines, hydrodynamic devices, a shaft generator, frequency inverters and silicone paint, amongst other energy efficiency improvements. The set of technologies applied will reduce GHG emissions by around 15% compared to the current generation of Guaibamax.

These technologies and alternative fuels are being tested as part of the Ecoshipping program, a research and development initiative created by Vale to support the maritime industry’s decarbonization efforts and improve the efficiency of the mining company’s fleet. Vale’s chartered fleet includes first-generation Valemax vessels since 2011, second-generation Valemax vessels since 2018 and, since 2019, the first generation of Guaibamax. These vessels are already among the most efficient in the world and can reduce CO2 equivalent emissions by up to 41% compared to a standard capesize vessel.

title: Now more than ever, biofuels show their value - Minnesota Reformer
authors: Brian Werner, Sarah Montalbano, John Phelan, Geoff Tolley, Thomas Legg
description:
Gasoline prices are climbing.
The war in Iran has created instability in oil markets and driven fuel prices up across the country.
A new study from the Minnesota Bio-Fuels Association examining more than a decade of fuel price and consumption data shows that E15, a gasoline blend with 15% ethanol and often marketed as Unleaded 88, is delivering measurable savings for Minnesota drivers.
The results are clear: E15 has consistently been priced lower than E10 every year since entering the Minnesota market.
It is a tangible way to help families manage their budgets while supporting jobs and economic activity across Minnesota.
text:
Gasoline prices are climbing. The war in Iran has created instability in oil markets and driven fuel prices up across the country. ​In Minnesota, gas prices have jumped roughly 50 cents in the last month according to AAA, and analysts warn continued instability in shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz could push them even higher in the weeks ahead.

For families already dealing with higher grocery bills, rising utility costs and housing payments, another spike at the pump is the last thing they need. When global energy markets become volatile, drivers here at home have little control over what they end up paying.

That is why affordability matters more than ever, and why it is worth paying attention to one place where Minnesotans are still finding real relief: E15 at the fuel pump.

A new study from the Minnesota Bio-Fuels Association examining more than a decade of fuel price and consumption data shows that E15, a gasoline blend with 15% ethanol and often marketed as Unleaded 88, is delivering measurable savings for Minnesota drivers. In 2024 alone, Minnesotans saved $24.7 million by choosing E15 instead of traditional E10 gasoline. Since 2013, cumulative savings total $79.5 million.

The analysis compares actual fuel prices and sales volumes from 2013 through 2024 and estimates what drivers would have paid if E15 had not been available. The results are clear: E15 has consistently been priced lower than E10 every year since entering the Minnesota market. In 2024, the price difference reached its largest point on record, with E15 priced up to 18 cents per gallon less than E10.

Consumers are noticing. The share of total gasoline sales represented by E15 has grown from virtually zero in 2013 to 5.6% in 2024, reflecting strong consumer demand for a lower-cost option.

When Minnesotans have access to a cheaper fuel choice, they use it.

The benefits do not stop with individual drivers. The same study finds that E15 sales and the consumer savings they generate contribute $166.3 million annually to Minnesota’s economy. That activity supports 1,081 jobs across agriculture, fuel retail, transportation and related supply-chain industries. It also generates $30.8 million in annual tax revenue that supports local, county, state and federal governments.

Infrastructure and vehicle readiness further strengthens the case. Any light-duty car, SUV, or light truck manufactured in model year 2001 or newer can use E15, and more than 550 stations across Minnesota offer E15 today. Most retail sites already have compatible infrastructure, with 77% of fuel stations having at least one underground storage tank that can accommodate E15. Much of the groundwork to expand access already exists.

Fuel costs ripple through the broader economy. When drivers spend less at the pump, they have more disposable income to spend on everything else. Small businesses benefit when transportation and delivery costs are more manageable. Farmers, truck drivers and retail workers all play a role in the value chain that supports E15 production and sales.

Global events also highlight another important point: E15 is produced here at home. Ethanol is made from American-grown corn and blended with gasoline at facilities across the country, including many in the Midwest. Expanding access to fuels like E15 gives consumers more affordable choices while extending our fuel supply and strengthening domestic energy security.

As policymakers consider how to address affordability concerns, it is important to recognize what is already working. E15 is a proven, market-based option delivering real savings right now. Protecting consistent access to E15 and expanding that access nationwide year-round, particularly during periods of high fuel demand, helps ensure that Minnesotans and all Americans can continue to benefit from a lower-priced fuel choice.

In a time of persistent cost pressures and global energy uncertainty, expanding access to lower-priced fuel is not an abstract policy debate. It is a tangible way to help families manage their budgets while supporting jobs and economic activity across Minnesota. The data show that E15 is doing both.

That is what fueling affordability for Minnesotans looks like in practice: measurable savings at the pump, broader economic benefits across the state, and greater energy security from a fuel produced here at home.

text:
Brazilian mining giant Vale is pushing the boundaries of maritime decarbonization with plans to deploy the world’s first ocean-going vessel powered primarily by ethanol—a move that could slash greenhouse gas emissions by up to 90%.

The company announced it has signed an agreement with Shandong Shipping Corporation to build a new generation of “Guaibamax” bulk carriers, marking the first time ethanol will be used as the main fuel on a deep-sea vessel. The first ship is expected to enter service in 2029.

The vessels will be massive by any standard—stretching 340 meters in length with a carrying capacity of 325,000 tonnes—and will feature a flexible, multi-fuel design. In addition to ethanol, they will be capable of running on methanol and conventional bunker fuel, with future retrofit options for LNG and ammonia.

Vale says the real breakthrough lies in ethanol’s emissions profile. When assessed on a full lifecycle “well-to-wake” basis, second-generation ethanol could cut carbon emissions by around 90% compared to traditional heavy fuel oil, the industry’s dominant fuel.

The project forms part of Vale’s broader strategy to decarbonize its logistics chain, particularly the shipping segment, which represents a major share of its Scope 3 emissions. The company has already committed to reducing these emissions by 15% by 2035.

“This is about combining flexibility and efficiency,” said Rodrigo Bermelho, Vale’s Director of Shipping. “Using ethanol alongside wind-assisted propulsion puts us in a strong position for the energy transition.”

Each vessel will also be equipped with five rotor sails to harness wind energy, along with a suite of efficiency upgrades including optimized hull design, shaft generators, advanced coatings, and frequency-controlled systems. Collectively, these improvements are expected to reduce emissions by an additional 15% compared to the current generation of Very Large Ore Carriers (VLOCs).

The ethanol-powered ships will follow a series of 10 dual-fuel (methanol and heavy fuel oil) vessels already on order from Shandong, scheduled for delivery starting in 2027.

The initiative is part of Vale’s “Ecoshipping” program, a long-running R&D effort aimed at accelerating maritime decarbonization. Since 2020, the company has invested approximately $1.4 billion in emissions reduction across its operations, including trials of ethanol in trucks and locomotives.

While alternative fuels like ammonia and methanol have dominated industry headlines, Vale’s ethanol bet introduces a new contender—one that could leverage existing biofuel supply chains while offering near-term emissions reductions.

If successful, the project could open a new pathway for bulk shipping’s energy transition—one fueled not just by innovation, but by a surprising source: alcohol.

text:
Quiet power

Understanding what a PEM fuel cell does, and why it represents such a departure from conventional shipboard power generation, is essential context. Since the earliest days of steam, power at sea has meant heat, noise, and rotation. A fuel pump starts clicking, cylinders begin firing, a crankshaft turns. That mechanical rhythm has defined the engineroom for over a century. A PEM fuel cell breaks every part of that convention.

At its heart, the process is electrochemical rather than thermal. Hydrogen enters one side of a thin polymer membrane, the membrane itself being a specialised material, typically Nafion or a comparable perfluoro‑sulphonic acid polymer, only a fraction of a millimetre thick yet highly selective in what it allows to pass. Oxygen from compressed air enters the other side. A platinum catalyst at the anode strips hydrogen molecules of their electrons. The protons migrate through the membrane under an electrochemical potential gradient, while the electrons are forced around an external electrical circuit, generating direct current before recombining with oxygen at the cathode to form water vapour. The entire exhaust product is water. No CO2, no SOx, no particulate matter, and at cruise loads, almost no noise beyond the hum of air compressors and cooling circuits.

“Batteries are invariably incorporated alongside fuel-cell stacks”

The efficiency advantage over combustion is real but requires qualification. A diesel generator converts fuel energy to electricity at perhaps 35–42% thermal efficiency under favourable conditions. A PEM fuel cell operating at design load can achieve electrical efficiencies of 50–60% because it bypasses the thermodynamic losses inherent in converting heat to mechanical work. At the steady hotel loads that dominate a cruise ship’s energy budget, this advantage is practically significant. It diminishes under dynamic conditions, which is one reason why batteries are invariably incorporated alongside fuel-cell stacks in marine installations: they absorb the rapid load transients that would otherwise force the fuel cell away from its optimal operating point.

The balance of plant surrounding the fuel cell – the air compressors, humidifiers, cooling circuits, power electronics and gas management systems – represents much of the real engineering challenge. PEM membranes must be maintained within a narrow window of temperature and humidity. Too little moisture and the membrane dries out, driving up electrical resistance and reducing output; too much and the cathode floods, starving the reaction of oxygen. Maintaining that balance aboard a moving vessel, with varying sea conditions, fluctuating loads, and the vibration environment of a working ship, demands sophisticated monitoring and control systems that are unique in a conventional engineroom.

A culture change in the engineroom

For engineers raised on rotating machinery, the cultural adjustment is considerable. A diesel generator can be coaxed through poor fuel quality, pushed through load steps with a cloud of black smoke, and nursed along while a fault is diagnosed. A fuel cell is less forgiving. Its protective logic is designed to prevent thermal hotspots and hydrogen accumulation, and the consequence of a serious fault is typically an abrupt shutdown rather than a gradual decline.

Redundancy must therefore be engineered in from the outset through multiple parallel stacks, and the energy management software that balances output between stacks, batteries and any remaining conventional generators takes on a role previously filled by the judgement of an experienced watch engineer. The maintenance culture shifts accordingly: no piston overhauls, no turbocharger balancing, no fuel injection timing, but instead tracking voltage degradation across stacks, ensuring air filtration systems remain clean, and maintaining cooling circuits with the precision usually associated with high‑power electronics.

Storage is one of the biggest challenges in using hydrogen as a fuel. Although hydrogen carries a lot of energy for its weight, its volumetric energy density is catastrophically low, so it takes up a huge amount of space. To store enough of it on a ship, it must either be compressed into very high‑pressure tanks at somewhere between 350 and 700 bar, or cooled to extremely low temperatures of about -253°C to become liquid. Both options are complex, very energy‑intensive and demand insulated cryogenic vessels with continuous boil‑off management systems to handle the inevitable heat ingress. This requires specialised equipment and makes storage far more difficult than with conventional marine fuels.

“A fuel cell is less forgiving”

Viking and Fincantieri have addressed the bunkering logistics challenge through a containerised approach to hydrogen storage and loading; a system designed to allow hydrogen to be delivered and loaded in standardised units without requiring the shore‑side infrastructure investment of a permanent cryogenic terminal at every port of call. The practical ingenuity of that solution should not be underestimated.

The environmental credentials of the system depend entirely on a question that sits well upstream of the ship itself: where did the hydrogen come from? The maritime industry has adopted a colour‑coding shorthand that illuminates the issue. Grey hydrogen, which accounts for most of global production, is manufactured by reacting natural gas with steam in a process known as steam methane reforming, producing hydrogen and roughly 9–12 kg of CO2 for every kilogram of hydrogen. Blue hydrogen follows the same route but captures a proportion of the CO2, and the carbon storage infrastructure adds considerable cost and complexity. Green hydrogen removes fossil fuels from the equation entirely, splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using electrolysis powered by renewable electricity. If that electricity is genuinely low‑carbon, the resulting hydrogen can approach true zero‑emissions status across its entire lifecycle.

That lifecycle view is now central to how IMO regulates the industry. The Net‑Zero Framework approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 measures greenhouse gas fuel intensity on a well‑to‑wake basis, tracing emissions from primary production all the way through to onboard consumption. The old tank‑to‑wake approach counted only what emerged from the exhaust stack; the switch to well‑to‑wake was a deliberate regulatory choice designed to prevent upstream emissions being laundered through low‑carbon conversion steps at the point of use. Grey hydrogen consumed in a fuel cell that emits only water vapour is not, under this framework, a low‑carbon solution. Green hydrogen, produced from renewable electricity, can achieve a near‑zero well‑to‑wake score and qualify for the compliance incentives built into the mechanism. The regulatory architecture is aligned with the physics.

The economics currently favour grey hydrogen by a considerable margin. Green hydrogen costs between three and eight dollars per kilogram to produce, against one to two dollars for the grey variety, and the infrastructure required for cryogenic storage and delivery adds further to the delivered cost. The premium over conventional marine fuels is real and substantial. Yet electrolyser costs are falling at a pace that has consistently surprised analysts, renewable electricity is becoming cheaper across every major market, and carbon pricing mechanisms are progressively tightening the financial case for high‑emissions fuels.

Viking acknowledged the current cost differential explicitly when announcing the project, while stating confidence that prices would fall over time. That is not an evasion; it is the same trajectory calculation that drove investment in LNG a decade ago, now applied to a fuel with genuinely better emissions credentials when produced cleanly.

Fincantieri CEO, Pierroberto Folgiero, framed the project’s significance from the shipbuilder’s perspective: “With Viking Libra, we are not only delivering the world’s first cruise ship powered by hydrogen stored on board, but also reinforcing our commitment to shaping the future of sustainable maritime transportation.” That distinction – hydrogen stored on board for both propulsion and electricity generation, not merely trialled as an auxiliary – is the engineering threshold that separates Viking Libra from earlier demonstration projects.

The containerised storage system, the 6‑MW fuel-cell installation, and the integration of liquefied hydrogen into the operational profile of a commercial passenger vessel represent a new level of commitment to the technology.

When Viking Libra enters service it will generate operational data on fuel-cell stack durability, hydrogen consumption rates, bunkering logistics, maintenance cycles and the response of PEM systems to the real‑world conditions of a working passenger ship. That evidence base does not currently exist anywhere in the industry at this scale. Industry will be watching the operational record closely. So will every cruise operator that is considering a hydrogen newbuilding programme.

title: Vale Ethanol Ships: Maritime Decarbonisation Pioneer - Discovery Alert
description:
Vale ethanol-powered ships represent a groundbreaking approach to maritime decarbonisation that could reshape international commodity transport.
Ethanol combustion produces zero sulfur oxide emissions, directly addressing International Maritime Organisation regulations that limit marine fuel sulfur content to 0.50% by mass.
The European Union's Emissions Trading System expansion incorporates maritime shipping as of January 1, 2024.
Global Ethanol Market Implications Supply Chain Infrastructure Development Maritime ethanol demand projections estimate 2-3 million tons annual consumption by 2035 as shipping industry adoption accelerates.
Crew safety and training effectiveness measurements evaluate human factors integration with ethanol fuel systems.
text:
The global shipping industry faces an unprecedented convergence of environmental regulation, technological advancement, and economic pressure that is fundamentally altering how bulk commodities reach international markets. Vale ethanol-powered ships represent a groundbreaking approach to maritime decarbonisation that could reshape international commodity transport. Traditional heavy fuel oil propulsion systems, which have dominated maritime transport for decades, are rapidly becoming incompatible with emerging carbon reduction mandates and customer sustainability requirements.

This transformation extends far beyond simple fuel substitution. Mining companies, steel manufacturers, and shipping operators are recognising that maritime decarbonisation represents a strategic imperative that will determine competitive positioning in carbon-conscious global markets. The integration of renewable fuels into transoceanic transport creates complex technical challenges whilst opening new pathways for operational efficiency and regulatory compliance, driving renewable energy transformations across the sector.

Understanding Maritime Fuel Evolution and Environmental Impact

Ethanol's Technical Advantages in Marine Applications

Ethanol presents unique characteristics that position it as a compelling alternative to conventional marine fuels. Life-cycle assessments demonstrate that sugarcane-derived ethanol achieves 80-90% carbon reduction compared to heavy fuel oil when accounting for production, transportation, and combustion phases. This dramatic improvement stems from ethanol's renewable feedstock origins and cleaner combustion properties.

The environmental benefits extend beyond carbon emissions. Ethanol combustion produces zero sulfur oxide emissions, directly addressing International Maritime Organisation regulations that limit marine fuel sulfur content to 0.50% by mass. Additionally, ethanol's biodegradability exceeds 90% in marine environments within 28 days under aerobic conditions, significantly reducing environmental persistence compared to petroleum-based fuels.

Fuel Characteristic Ethanol Heavy Fuel Oil Methanol Ammonia Carbon Reduction Potential 80-90% Baseline 70-85% 95%+ Sulfur Content Zero 0.5% max Zero Zero Marine Biodegradability >90% (28 days) <30% (28 days) >85% (28 days) Variable Infrastructure Compatibility High Standard Medium Low Energy Density (MJ/kg) 29.7 46.0 22.7 18.6

Operational Considerations and Technical Challenges

Ethanol's lower energy density compared to heavy fuel oil requires approximately 35-40% larger fuel tank volumes for equivalent voyage range. This constraint affects vessel design and cargo capacity allocation, particularly important for bulk carriers maximising payload efficiency. Ethanol's hygroscopic nature necessitates specialised tank coatings and water removal systems to prevent corrosion of fuel system components.

The dual-fuel engine systems being developed for ethanol applications incorporate compression ignition modifications whilst maintaining operational flexibility. These systems allow seamless switching between ethanol and conventional fuels during infrastructure development phases, ensuring operational continuity across global trade routes.

Safety considerations favour ethanol over other alternative marine fuels. Unlike methanol or ammonia, ethanol presents relatively low toxicity risks during fuel handling operations and accidental spillage scenarios. This characteristic reduces crew training requirements and occupational health compliance costs compared to more hazardous alternative fuels.

Regulatory Framework Driving Maritime Transformation

The International Maritime Organisation established a 40% carbon intensity reduction target by 2030 (baseline 2008), with further requirements for 70% reductions by 2050. These targets apply to all vessels above 5,000 gross tonnage engaged in international trade, directly affecting bulk carrier operations transporting iron ore, coal, and other commodities.

The European Union's Emissions Trading System expansion incorporates maritime shipping as of January 1, 2024. Shipping companies must surrender allowances for 100% of verified emissions from voyages starting or ending in EU ports by 2026, rising from 40% in 2024. Under current allowance pricing of approximately €75-85 per ton of CO₂, a Capesize vessel's annual transport emissions could incur €500,000-700,000 in compliance costs.

Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms

The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, entering full application in January 2026, applies to imports of iron ore, steel, cement, aluminium, and fertilisers. Embedded maritime transport emissions within these commodities affect pricing structures and procurement decisions, creating direct financial incentives for low-carbon transportation methods.

Port state control enforcement has expanded detention authority for vessels non-compliant with environmental standards. The Paris Memorandum of Understanding reported 3.2% detention rates for environmental non-compliance among inspected vessels in 2023, demonstrating increased regulatory scrutiny.

Economic Incentives Accelerating Adoption

Marine insurers provide documented 5-12% premium reductions for vessels meeting advanced environmental performance standards. Priority berthing arrangements at major ports can reduce vessel idle time by 2-5 days per port call, translating to €50,000-150,000 in operational savings per vessel annually.

Customer environmental, social, and governance requirements increasingly influence procurement decisions. Approximately 68% of major commodity buyers now incorporate supply chain carbon metrics into procurement evaluations, creating market pressure for sustainably transported materials.

Vale Ethanol-Powered Ships Strategic Initiative

Fleet Modernisation Timeline and Specifications

Vale's comprehensive fleet transformation involves multiple phases integrating different alternative fuel technologies. The company has announced charter agreements for 10 dual-fuel Guaibamax vessels capable of running on methanol and heavy fuel oil, with deliveries scheduled between 2027 and 2029 through partnerships with Shandong Shipping Corporation.

The pioneering ethanol-powered vessel programme includes two dedicated Guaibamax-class ships scheduled for operational deployment beginning 2029. Each vessel carries 325,000 metric tons of iron ore capacity, representing the largest conventional bulk carriers capable of transiting major global trade routes without specialised canal arrangements.

Advanced efficiency technologies integrated into these Vale ethanol-powered ships include:

Rotor sail wind energy harvesting systems generating propulsive force from wind energy

Enhanced engine designs delivering 15-20% fuel consumption reduction versus conventional Capesize vessels

Dual-fuel capability maintaining operational flexibility during infrastructure development

Optimised hull designs maximising cargo capacity whilst accommodating enlarged fuel storage requirements

Partnership Strategy and Risk Management

The 25-year charter commitment with Shandong Shipping Corporation demonstrates confidence in ethanol's long-term viability whilst providing stability needed for infrastructure development and technology refinement. This extended timeframe allows amortisation of initial capital premiums across vessel operational lifecycles.

Vale's approach incorporates conversion feasibility studies for existing methanol fleet vessels to ethanol capability, creating potential pathways for broader fleet integration. The company operates approximately 50 Guaibamax vessels within its current shipping operations, representing significant scaling potential for alternative fuel adoption.

Risk mitigation strategies include:

Operational flexibility through dual-fuel engine capability

Technology upgrade pathways built into charter contracts

Performance guarantees protecting against early-stage technical risks

Diversified fuel options reducing dependence on single alternative fuel sources

Technical Implementation Challenges and Solutions

Engine Technology Adaptations

The Winterthur Gas & Diesel ME-LGI engine platform represents the primary marine propulsion system designed for fuel-flexible operation, with capacity ratings up to 18,270 kW per unit in large bulk carrier applications. These systems require specific modifications for ethanol injection and combustion optimisation.

Dual-fuel engines maintain combustion reliability across ethanol's octane rating of approximately 100-105 compared to heavy fuel oil specifications. Corrosion-resistant materials throughout fuel systems address ethanol's different chemical properties and water absorption characteristics.

Enhanced combustion chamber designs optimise ethanol's burning characteristics whilst maintaining compatibility with conventional fuels. These modifications ensure operational flexibility during the infrastructure development phase when ethanol availability may be limited at certain ports.

Fuel Storage and Distribution Systems

Ethanol's 35-40% lower energy density compared to heavy fuel oil requires substantial modifications to vessel fuel storage arrangements. Tank design incorporates specialised coatings and water separation systems addressing ethanol's hygroscopic properties.

Temperature-controlled storage systems maintain fuel quality during extended voyages, particularly important for transoceanic routes between Brazil and Asian markets. Specialised bunkering equipment enables safe fuel transfer operations whilst maintaining compatibility with existing port infrastructure.

Crew training programmes address ethanol-specific handling procedures, safety protocols, and emergency response requirements. These programmes build upon existing chemical handling expertise whilst addressing ethanol's unique operational characteristics.

Global Ethanol Market Implications

Supply Chain Infrastructure Development

Maritime ethanol demand projections estimate 2-3 million tons annual consumption by 2035 as shipping industry adoption accelerates. Brazil's sugarcane ethanol production capacity, currently generating approximately 33 billion litres annually, provides established supply chain foundations for marine fuel applications.

Second-generation ethanol production from agricultural waste and cellulosic feedstocks represents emerging supply sources that could expand available volumes without competing with food production. These advanced biofuel pathways offer improved carbon reduction performance and greater feedstock sustainability.

Port terminal infrastructure development includes:

Dedicated ethanol storage facilities at major bunkering ports

Specialised bunkering vessel fleets for fuel transfer operations

Quality certification protocols ensuring marine fuel specifications

International standardisation enabling cross-border fuel trade

Competitive Response Patterns

Mining industry fleet decarbonisation initiatives demonstrate varied technological approaches reflecting different sustainability transformation strategies. BHP's partnerships with bp focus on marine biofuels, whilst Rio Tinto conducts hydrogen-powered vessel trials. Fortescue develops ammonia fuel applications, and Anglo American experiments with methanol shipping solutions.

Shipping companies pursue diverse alternative fuel strategies reflecting different risk tolerances and operational requirements. Maersk leads methanol vessel orders and operations, CMA CGM invests in LNG and biofuel systems, MSC researches hydrogen fuel cell applications, and COSCO develops multi-fuel operational capabilities.

Economic Analysis and Market Impact

Transportation Cost Evolution

Initial alternative fuel premiums range 10-15% above conventional heavy fuel oil, reflecting production costs, infrastructure limitations, and technology development expenses. Economic modelling suggests economies of scale will reduce cost differentials significantly by 2030 as production volumes increase and technology matures.

Total cost of ownership analysis incorporates fuel costs representing 50-60% of operating expenses, capital depreciation at 20-25%, crew wages at 15-20%, maintenance at 8-12%, and insurance at 3-5%. Alternative fuel adoption primarily affects the fuel component whilst potentially reducing other cost categories through efficiency improvements.

Carbon pricing integration into freight rates creates new pricing mechanisms reflecting environmental costs. Green premium pricing for sustainably transported commodities ranges 1-3% above conventional rates in specialty markets, with broader adoption expected as regulatory requirements expand.

Iron Ore Market Competitiveness

Vale's Brazilian iron ore maintains logistics advantages through proximity to Atlantic markets and established infrastructure. These Vale ethanol-powered ships reinforce competitive positions by reducing transportation carbon intensity and compliance costs compared to longer Pacific routes, directly influencing global iron ore dynamics.

Australian iron ore producers face different competitive dynamics due to longer voyage distances to European markets and reliance on different fuel supply chains. Chinese steel industry green procurement requirements increasingly influence supplier selection based on total carbon footprint including transportation emissions.

European steel sector carbon footprint regulations create direct demand for low-carbon transported raw materials. Steel producers including ArcelorMittal, ThyssenKrupp, and others have committed to carbon-neutral procurement by 2030-2040, creating supply chain pressure for sustainable transportation methods. This mirrors broader green iron production initiatives across the industry.

Performance Metrics and Success Indicators

Operational Performance Benchmarks

Key performance indicators for Vale ethanol-powered ships include fuel consumption efficiency compared to conventional vessels, carbon emission reductions achieved through operational deployment, and maintenance cost patterns relative to traditional propulsion systems. These metrics provide crucial data for broader industry adoption decisions.

Crew safety and training effectiveness measurements evaluate human factors integration with ethanol fuel systems. Customer satisfaction assessments determine market acceptance of sustainable transportation services and willingness to support premium pricing for low-carbon shipping.

Industry Adoption Tracking

Success measurements extend beyond individual vessel performance to industry-wide transformation indicators:

Number of ethanol-capable vessels entering global fleet operations

Port infrastructure development progress across major bunkering locations

Fuel price parity achievement timeline comparing ethanol to conventional fuels

Regulatory compliance cost savings quantifying operational benefits

Technology maturation rates reducing initial implementation risks

Strategic Implications for Maritime Decarbonisation

The convergence of environmental necessity, technological feasibility, and economic viability creates conditions for accelerated maritime fuel transformation. These pioneering applications represent critical developments within broader industry evolution trends that will generate operational data crucial for industry-wide decision making.

The 25-year charter commitment provides stability for infrastructure development whilst demonstrating confidence in ethanol's long-term viability as a marine fuel. Success in these initial deployments could catalyse broader adoption across bulk shipping operations, container vessels, and other maritime sectors.

Alternative fuel diversification strategies reduce operational risks whilst addressing different technical and economic constraints across vessel types and trade routes. The integration of multiple fuel options creates operational flexibility and supply chain resilience in an evolving regulatory environment.

Investment Considerations: Stakeholders evaluating maritime decarbonisation opportunities should consider technology maturation timelines, infrastructure development requirements, and regulatory compliance advantages when assessing different alternative fuel pathways. Early adoption provides competitive advantages but requires careful risk management during technology transition phases.

text:
LONDON: — A landmark study from the UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group and RMI has found that the inclusion of GHG pricing in the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO’s) policy framework will be critical in the shipping industry achieving a cost-effective energy transition.

The analysis shows that there are multiple benefits from GHG pricing, including a less volatile and more investable fuel market, improving the availability of compliant solutions, protecting countries from risks of policy-driven economic shocks, enabling early adoption of low-emissions fuels, and creating the revenue streams crucial for contributing to a just and equitable transition.

The results are publishing just as the IMO is about to reconvene at the 84th session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 84) to consider how to move forward policy ambitions after the decision to adopt the Net Zero Framework (NZF), a global policy framework for the shipping sector, was postponed in October 2025. The in-depth research shows that alternative policy architecture proposals removing GHG pricing and focusing on a technical-only solution will have negative impacts on the sector’s transition.

The findings come from a new fleet evolution modelling (FEM) framework from the UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group and RMI — the first of its kind to explicitly model several shipowner behaviours, including ‘peer influence’ on how they perceive different fuel options. The modelling was used to evaluate both the NZF, approved in principle at MEPC 83 last year, along with other policy architectures that have been proposed as a way forwards in the event the negotiations on architecture are reopened. The results reveal critical differences in the ability to invest in the transition for early adopters and fuel producers based on policy choices.

Dr Marie Fricaudet, Senior Research Fellow at UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group said: “This research fills a critical gap in the evidence base. By modelling how mass market shipowners actually make decisions — cautiously, with limited foresight, and with one eye on their competitors — we get a fundamentally different picture of what different policy architectures and GHG pricing will deliver.”

What the fleet evolution model reveals for policy design

Applied to five foreseeable IMO policy architectures, the model produces findings that differ meaningfully from existing approaches:

Regional policy alone cannot drive global fleet transition. A ‘no IMO, EU only’ scenario shows no evidence of driving energy transition in the global fleet. Most vessels have limited exposure to EU regulation, so those policies alone don’t change investment decisions — reinforcing the imperative for a robust global IMO measure.

The transition will start slowly — then accelerate quickly. Most shipowners will wait until a critical mass adopts new fuels. However, once that tipping point is reached, including peer effects can drive rapid, self-reinforcing shifts that can put pressure on fuel supply chains. Policymakers should plan for both the slow-start to transition and the acceleration.

Policy design determines investability. Only architectures combining a GHG price, a capped SU market, and a reward mechanism for zero- and near-zero (ZNZ) fuels create the conditions for an investable transition. Uncapped SU supply, as arises under a technical-only measure, generates price volatility that deters the investment the policy is meant to unlock.

Early adopter support is critical, not optional. Mass market actors will not move until early adopters have demonstrated a technology pathway. Without reward mechanisms to incentivise early ZNZ uptake, first movers won’t invest. Failing to support early adopters in policy design carries significant transition risk.

Price stability requires deliberate design. Even under the NZF, credit prices could become unstable if too many rewards or multipliers create a surplus of units too quickly. If governments then step in to keep prices artificially low — below the real cost of compliance — it would weaken the business case for investing in clean fuels and disrupt the very markets the policy is meant to support.

Fuel availability is as decisive as fuel cost. Supply constraints can slow adoption even when alternative fuels are economically viable. Rapid demand surges — particularly for ammonia in high biofuel price scenarios — may outpace production, Strong revenue support for early fuel investment is critical to avoid these bottlenecks.

Modelling innovations in this study

Existing models used in IMO policy debates have typically assumed shipowners have perfect foresight and minimise costs rationally, and that surplus unit (SU) prices are fixed or modelled independently of fleet behaviour. This research demonstrates that neither holds, and addresses both through two key innovations:

Realistic mass market behaviour. Drawing on interviews with 16 shipowners, the model distinguishes early adopters from mass market actors (95% of the fleet). Most shipowners are modelled as risk-averse, with shorter planning horizons and a tendency to follow others — investing most confidently when around 20% of the fleet has done so. This produces non-linear adoption dynamics and tipping points that conventional models often miss.

Dynamic SU market modelling. Rather than assuming a fixed SU price, the model calculates SU supply and demand across the fleet at each time step to determine a market price. This creates a feedback loop — investment decisions today affect SU prices tomorrow, which in turn shape future investment — mirroring how the NZF and other architectures would operate in practice.

Ruosida Lin, Modelling & Analytics Lead at RMI climate aligned industry program shipping team said: “By linking individual shipowner behaviour to sector-wide dynamics, this research offers a bottom-up view of the shipping transition. It shows how cautious, competitive decisions shape market outcomes and policy effectiveness. We see this as an advancement over traditional modelling and look forward to building on this further.”

Implications for the NZF architecture

The analysis offers a direct comparative assessment of the four candidate IMO policy architectures:

The NZF ‘as is’ contains the key structural features needed for an investable transition: a capped SU market and a reward mechanism. Careful design of reward rates, multipliers and review mechanisms will be needed to manage SU price volatility.

A levy combined with a Greenhouse Gas Fuel Intensity (GFI) limit offers the same structural features with a simpler, more predictable revenue architecture and greater flexibility to fund a just and equitable transition.

A single-tier GFI can provide a capped SU market but introduces risks of SU price instability if the regulatory unit (RU) price must balance both compliance incentives and revenue generation simultaneously.

A technical-only measure delivers none of the above. It leaves the SU market uncapped, provides no revenue for rewards or just transition, and — on the evidence of this modelling — carries the highest transition risk and cost of any architecture considered.

A well-designed global framework that reflects real-world investment behaviour, and that rewards early action and ensures price stability, can unlock the momentum needed to scale clean fuels across the shipping sector. As the IMO moves toward finalizing its Net Zero Framework, the right policy decisions can help the sector achieve a timely, cost-effective, just and equitable transition.

title: Fill 'er up with methanol: Kandla port's landmark trial puts India on the global green fuel map
description:
Earlier this month, a routine-looking fuel transfer on the Gujarat coast turned into a historic moment for Indian shipping.
Deendayal Port Authority (DPA), Kandla, India's single largest port by cargo volume, completed the country's first-ever shore-to-ship methanol bunkering trial, pumping methanol directly from shore tanks into a vessel in a demonstration.
The next phase will involve ship-to-ship methanol bunkering at high seas.

text:
Earlier this month, a routine-looking fuel transfer on the Gujarat coast turned into a historic moment for Indian shipping. Deendayal Port Authority (DPA), Kandla, India's single largest port by cargo volume, completed the country's first-ever shore-to-ship methanol bunkering trial, pumping methanol directly from shore tanks into a vessel in a demonstration.

According to maritime experts, this is a critical early step in cleaning up the world's dirtiest-emitting industry. Think of methanol bunkering the same way you'd think of filling up your car, except the "car" is a 300-metre deep-sea cargo ship, the "petrol station" is an entire port terminal, and the fuel being pumped produces dramatically fewer emissions than the conventional heavy fuel oil that ships have burned since the 19th century.

Methanol emits roughly 10–15 per cent less CO₂ and virtually no sulphur oxides compared to traditional bunker fuel, and when it's the "e-methanol" variety made from renewable energy and captured CO₂, the emissions are even cleaner.

The trial was conducted in collaboration with Stolt Tankers, J M Baxi, Aegis Vopak and Indian Oil Corporation Ltd (IOCL), and was independently verified on-site by DNV Maritime Advisory Services, one of the world's top maritime classification bodies.

DNV's assessment found Kandla to be at Level 6 on the IAPH Port Readiness Level (PRL) scale, which, on a 1-to-9 scale (where 1–3 is analysis, 4–6 is development, and 7–9 is implementation), puts Kandla solidly in the advanced development category, with verified infrastructure ready to support commercial methanol bunkering.

And Kandla's ambitions don't stop at a trial. The port is targeting availability of around 500,000 tonnes per annum of RFNBO-compliant e-methanol by 2028–29, targeting a competitive price of $700–$750 per metric tonne, aimed at dual-fuel vessels plying the busy Asia–Europe trade corridor, one of the world's most important shipping lanes.

DPA has also initiated site work for India's first 150-tonnes-per-day e-methanol plant in partnership with Assam Petrochemicals and Thermax, and has issued tenders for a port-integrated biomethanol production facility. The next phase will involve ship-to-ship methanol bunkering at high seas.

Maersk, the world's second-largest shipping company, has already ordered 25 methanol-powered vessels and is sourcing 500,000 tonnes/year of green methanol. The IMO wants net-zero shipping emissions by 2050. Kandla, sitting right on the Rotterdam–Singapore green shipping corridor, is positioning India to be the fill-up stop of choice for the next generation of clean ships.

text:
Norway is set to transform coastal transport with the introduction of “flying” electric ferries, as operator Boreal AS places an order for 20 Candela P-12 hydrofoil vessels.

The landmark deal represents the largest electric passenger vessel fleet ever commissioned and signals a major leap forward for zero-emission maritime travel.

High-Speed Electric Travel Comes to the Fjords

With its vast coastline and reliance on water-based transport, Norway has long faced challenges in electrifying high-speed ferries. While the country leads globally in electric car adoption—where nearly all new car sales are fully electric—fast passenger vessels have remained dependent on diesel due to limitations in speed and range.

The Candela P-12 changes that equation. Capable of cruising at 25 knots with a range of approximately 40 nautical miles, the vessel enables fully electric operation on routes that were previously only viable with fossil fuels. The deployment of 20 vessels is expected to increase service frequency and significantly reduce travel times along Norway’s fjord-lined coast.

Hydrofoil Technology Unlocks Efficiency

At the heart of the P-12’s performance is its advanced hydrofoil system. Computer-controlled underwater wings lift the vessel above the water at speeds exceeding 18 knots, dramatically reducing drag. This design cuts energy consumption by up to 80 percent compared to conventional ferries of similar size.

The result is not only improved efficiency but also lower operational costs and reduced environmental impact—key factors for scaling electric maritime transport.

Fast Charging Without Heavy Infrastructure

One of the P-12’s biggest advantages is its ability to recharge using standard DC fast chargers, similar to those used for electric cars. The vessel can fully recharge in about an hour, eliminating the need for expensive megawatt-scale charging infrastructure typically required by electric ferries.

This capability has already been demonstrated in real-world conditions, including a record-setting electric sea journey between Sweden and Norway, where the vessel recharged using a mobile battery system.

Quiet, Smooth, and Passenger-Friendly

Passenger comfort is another major focus. The P-12 is equipped with a digital flight control system that continuously adjusts the hydrofoils based on wave conditions, ensuring a smooth ride even in rough waters.

Noise levels are also remarkably low. Tests in Stockholm recorded cabin noise at just 64 dB—quieter than many trains, aircraft, and traditional ferries—making it one of the most silent high-speed vessels in operation.

Delivery Timeline and Future Impact

The first two vessels are scheduled for delivery in 2027, with the remaining fleet arriving in stages between 2028 and 2030. Boreal plans to deploy the ferries on multiple routes across Norway, with potential expansion into international markets.

This initiative highlights how innovative technology and forward-thinking operators can accelerate the transition to zero-emission transport—not just on roads, but across waterways as well.

As Norway continues to lead in electrification, the rollout of electric hydrofoil ferries could serve as a blueprint for sustainable maritime travel worldwide.

The Brazilian miner Vale and Shandong Shipping Corporation have concluded a charter agreement for new Guaibamax grade vessels, powered by ethanol, with first unit to be delivered in 2029.

According to Vale, the agreement is an unprecedented milestone for global iron ore transportation, as it is the first time in maritime industry that ethanol will be adopted as the primary fuel on a transoceanic vessel.

With the potential to reduce carbon emissions by approximately 90 percent, compared with the usual heavy fuel oil, the initiative reinforces Vale's commitment to reducing its carbon emissions in the value chain and promoting decarbonization in the maritime sector, in line with ongoing discussions at the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

The agreement between Vale and Shandong includes 25-year contracts for the construction of two ships, with an option for more vessels.

The adoption of these second-generation Guaibamax vessels, which are 340 meters long and have a capacity of 325,000 metric tons, is part of Vale’s multi-fuel strategy.

In addition to ethanol, these vessels will be able to use methanol and heavy oil, while the design also allows for conversion to liquefied natural gas (LNG) or ammonia.

Considering the complete fuel cycle from well to propeller (well-to-wake), so-called “second generation ethanol” can represent a reduction of approximately 90% in carbon emissions compared with heavy oil.

In addition to maritime transportation, Vale's adoption of ethanol in logistics includes tests in trucks during operations and in locomotives on the Vitória-Minas Railway (EFVM).

text:
Conceptual Diagram of MOL-Shell Book and Claim Model. Image Credit: MOL

Japan’s shipping firm Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (MOL) has teamed up with energy firm Shell to pilot a book and claim system aimed at cutting shipping emissions.

Under the initiative, Shell Trading Rotterdam B.V supplied a marine biofuel to a vessel not operated by MOL, replacing VLSFO, MOL said in a statement on its website on Thursday.

While the vessel operator kept the emissions savings linked to its own operations, it gave up the portion tied to cargo owners.

Shell then recorded these emissions savings in a registry run by 123Carbon and transferred them to MOL.

MOL converted the savings into Environmental Attribute Certificates (EACs), which it can offer to customers through its low-carbon shipping programme.

The model allows companies to claim emissions reductions even if the low-carbon marine fuel is used on a different ship, helping expand access to greener transport options.

Both companies said the trial shows how collaboration can support wider adoption of low-carbon fuels across the shipping sector.
